The smudge filter is what turns a pointer into the real file, and it only runs if the filter is configured **before** the working tree is written. `git lfs env` reporting the filter as installed for the repo is misleading: `git lfs install --local` writes into `.git/config`, which does not exist until after the clone has already checked out. So a fresh clone on a machine with no global LFS config produces pointers, then you install the filter, then `git lfs pull` fixes it after the fact.

Two things to check locally:

```bash
git lfs install            # writes filter.lfs.* into ~/.gitconfig, once per machine
git config --get-regexp '^filter\.lfs'
echo "$GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE"   # if this is 1, clone deliberately leaves pointers
```

In CI the cause is different and simpler: `actions/checkout` does not fetch LFS objects unless you ask.

```bash
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    lfs: true
```

That makes checkout run `git lfs fetch` + `git lfs checkout` after the clone, so the files are real by the time your build step runs.

Two things that will bite you afterwards:

- Do not put the working tree or `.git/lfs` into `actions/cache`. A restored cache can contain pointer files that the smudge filter will not re-resolve, and you get the same symptom with no obvious cause.
- LFS bandwidth on GitHub is metered separately from Actions minutes. If only a few large assets matter, `lfs: false` plus an explicit `git lfs pull --include="assets/hero.psd"` fetches one file instead of the whole store.

`filter-branch` does not delete anything — it writes new commits and leaves every old commit reachable through backup refs, which is deliberate so you can undo it. Three things keep your blob alive:

1. `refs/original/*`, the backup refs filter-branch created.
2. The reflogs (`HEAD` and every branch), which count as reachability roots for `gc`.
3. Any packed object that has not been pruned yet.

Full sequence:

```bash
git for-each-ref --format='delete %(refname)' refs/original \
  | git update-ref --stdin
git reflog expire --expire=now --expire-unreachable=now --all
git gc --prune=now
git cat-file -p 9a4c1f2   # should now say: Not a valid object name
```

Also check `git stash list` and any worktree — a stash holds objects too.

Two corrections worth making:

`filter-branch` is deprecated; git prints a warning telling you to use `git-filter-repo`. `filter-repo` deletes the backup refs and expires the reflog for you, so the cleanup above is not needed.

More importantly: **none of this matters for the secret itself.** Once the blob was pushed, it existed on GitHub's servers, was reachable by SHA over the API, was potentially fetched by CI, by forks, and by anyone watching the events firehose. Force-pushing removes it from the branch, not from history that others already have. GitHub does not garbage-collect unreachable objects on demand — you have to open a support request to have them dropped, and forks keep their own copy regardless. Treat the key as compromised: rotate it in IAM first, then do the history rewrite as cleanup.

`github.run_id` is unique to every run, so the primary key can never hit — you are writing a new cache entry on every run and never reading one back. That part is expected.

The reason `restore-keys: npm-` also misses is scoping. A cache written by a run on branch `feature/x` is readable from that branch and from branches created off it, but not from unrelated branches. Caches created on the default branch are readable everywhere. So if your first runs happened on a feature branch, another branch sees nothing, which reads as "the cache never works".

Key it on the lockfile instead:

```bash
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ runner.os }}-npm-
```

`hashFiles` changes only when dependencies change, so identical dependency sets share one entry, and `restore-keys` gives you a warm-but-stale `~/.npm` when they do change, which still saves most of the download.

Include `runner.os` — `~/.npm` from a macOS runner contains native builds that are wrong on Linux.

Simpler still, `setup-node` already does all of this:

```bash
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: 22
    cache: npm
```

Two limits to know: a cache entry is evicted after 7 days without a read, and the repository cache has a size cap (10 GB at the time of writing) with least-recently-used eviction, so a workflow that writes a new entry per run will evict its own useful ones.

This is intentional and not configurable: a `pull_request` run from a fork gets a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no secrets, because the workflow file *and* the code it runs come from the fork. If secrets were available, any stranger could open a PR whose build script prints them.

`pull_request_target` is the trigger people reach for next, and it does give you secrets — because it runs the workflow file from the **base** branch with the base repo's permissions. But if you then `actions/checkout` the PR head, you have handed fork-authored code your secrets. That is the well-known privilege escalation, not a fix.

The accepted pattern is a two-workflow split: an untrusted build with no secrets, then a trusted deploy triggered by `workflow_run`.

```bash
# .github/workflows/build.yml
on: pull_request
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/ }
```

```bash
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: [build]
    types: [completed]
permissions:
  actions: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  deploy:
    if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: preview
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: dist
          run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }}
          github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - run: ./upload.sh dist/
        env:
          TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
```

The second workflow runs from the default branch, so a fork cannot change it, and it only ever handles a build artifact — never executes fork code. Treat the downloaded artifact as untrusted data: publish it, do not run it. Adding `environment: preview` with required reviewers gives you a human gate on first-time contributors as well.

`include` without any other matrix keys declares the combinations directly instead of subtracting from a product:

```bash
strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    include:
      - os: ubuntu-latest
        node: 20
      - os: macos-latest
        node: 22
runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
steps:
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
    with:
      node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
```

Two jobs, no cross product. Each object under `include` is one job, and every key in it becomes a `matrix.*` value.

The behaviour that trips people up is `include` next to real matrix dimensions. There it is not "add these jobs" — it is: for each entry, if its keys can be merged into an already-generated combination without overwriting an original matrix value, it is merged into that combination; otherwise it is appended as a new job. So

```bash
matrix:
  os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
  include:
    - os: ubuntu-latest
      coverage: true
```

gives you two jobs, with `coverage` set only on the Linux one — not three. That merge rule is why `include` is the right tool for "same combinations, extra per-combination settings", and why include-only is the right tool for "just these pairs".

`exclude` is applied before `include`, so mixing all three to express two pairs is always going to be longer than listing the two pairs.

Also add `fail-fast: false` if you want both platforms' results on a failure; by default the first failure cancels the rest, which makes a two-job matrix considerably less useful.

The title is the clue: a 404 on the archive means the job asked for the artifact and the server no longer had it. `expire_in: 1 hour` is the cause.

Artifacts are deleted when they expire, whatever the pipeline state. If the `test` job did not start within the hour — a manual job, a job that waited for a free runner, a `retry` you clicked the next morning, a pipeline that sat in a queue behind others — the archive is gone by the time the download runs. In most runner versions that download failure is logged as a warning and the job continues, which is exactly why the first error you see is from `ls` rather than from the artifact step.

Confirm in the `test` job log, near the top, right after the git section:

```bash
Downloading artifacts for build (4821)...
WARNING: Downloading artifacts from coordinator... not found  id=4821 responseStatus=404 Not Found
```

If that line is missing entirely, it is a different problem (stage ordering or `needs`). If it is there with 404, it is expiry.

Fix:

```bash
build:
  stage: build
  script: npm run build
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/
    expire_in: 1 day

test:
  stage: test
  needs: [build]
  script: ls dist/
```

`expire_in: 1 day` is a saner floor — an hour only survives a pipeline that runs straight through. `needs: [build]` makes the dependency explicit; with it, a missing artifact is a hard failure with a clear message instead of a silent warning, which is what you want here. Note that `needs` also lets `test` start as soon as `build` finishes rather than waiting for the whole stage.

If you want the last good build to stay downloadable forever, GitLab keeps the most recent artifacts of the latest successful pipeline per ref regardless of `expire_in`, as long as "Keep artifacts from most recent successful jobs" is enabled in the project's CI settings.

`No URL provided, cache will not be downloaded from shared cache server` is the whole answer: the runner has no object-storage backend configured, so the cache lives as a tarball on the runner host's local disk (`/home/gitlab-runner/cache/...` for a shell executor). Runner A cannot read runner B's disk.

So today: when the same runner happens to pick up the job, the local tarball is there and you get a hit. When the other one does, you get a miss. That looks like "works within a pipeline, never across pipelines" because consecutive jobs in one pipeline often land on the same host.

Yes, a distributed cache is required as soon as more than one runner can take the job. Configure it in `config.toml` on **both** runners:

```bash
[runners.cache]
  Type = "s3"
  Shared = true
  [runners.cache.s3]
    ServerAddress = "s3.amazonaws.com"
    BucketName = "gitlab-runner-cache"
    BucketLocation = "eu-central-1"
    AuthenticationType = "iam"
```

`Shared = true` drops the runner token from the cache path, which is what makes an entry written by one runner visible to the other. Without it each runner still gets its own namespace in the bucket and nothing changes.

Two things worth fixing in the job at the same time:

```bash
cache:
  key:
    files:
      - package-lock.json
  paths:
    - .npm/

build:
  script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
    - npm run build
```

`npm ci` deletes `node_modules/` before installing, so caching `node_modules/` buys you nothing — the cache is extracted and then immediately wiped. Cache the npm download cache instead. And `key: files:` invalidates automatically when the lockfile changes; the default key is per-branch, which quietly gives every branch a cold cache.

The alternative, if you do not want object storage: pin these jobs to one host with a runner tag. It works, and it makes that host a single point of failure.

The shell executor does clean by default — `GIT_STRATEGY` unset means `fetch`, and fetch runs `git clean` with `GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS` defaulting to `-ffdx`, which removes untracked *and* ignored files. So `build/` should be wiped before every job.

The order of operations is what saves the stale files:

1. `git clean -ffdx` + fetch + checkout
2. **cache extraction**
3. artifact download
4. your script

Anything in `cache: paths:` is unpacked *after* the clean. If `build/` (or a parent of it) is in the cache, the job deletes it and then restores it from the previous job's tarball — and a file deleted from the repo three commits ago lives on in that tarball forever, because caches are extracted over the tree, never mirrored to it.

Check `.gitlab-ci.yml` for a `cache:` entry covering `build/` or `.`, and check the job log for `Successfully extracted cache` appearing before your script. Remove the output directory from the cache — build output is what `artifacts:` is for, not `cache:`.

If it is not the cache, the second candidate is an override:

```bash
variables:
  GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS: none     # someone added this to speed up builds
```

That disables the clean entirely and is the other way stale files persist on a shell executor.

For a belt-and-braces guarantee:

```bash
variables:
  GIT_STRATEGY: clone
  GIT_CLEAN_FLAGS: -ffdx

build:
  before_script:
    - rm -rf build
  script:
    - npm run build
```

`GIT_STRATEGY: clone` deletes the working directory and clones fresh each time. It costs you a full clone per job (mitigate with `GIT_DEPTH: 20`), but on a shell executor it is the closest thing to the container guarantee you are used to.

`Reader` is a control-plane role. It grants `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read` — you can see the account exists, read its properties, and list keys is a separate action again. It grants nothing under `.../blobServices/containers/blobs/*`, which is what a `GET` on the blob endpoint is authorised against. That is why the same code works with an account key: the key path bypasses Azure RBAC entirely.

The data-plane roles you want are the `Storage Blob Data *` family:

- `Storage Blob Data Reader` — read and list blobs
- `Storage Blob Data Contributor` — read, write, delete
- `Storage Blob Data Owner` — the above plus POSIX ACL management on ADLS Gen2

```bash
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id <managed-identity-principal-id> \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/<account>/blobServices/default/containers/<container>"
```

Scope it at the container if you can; account scope works too.

Use `--assignee-object-id` with `--assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal` for a managed identity. `--assignee` with the client id sometimes resolves against the wrong directory object and gives you an assignment that looks right in `az role assignment list` and does nothing.

Second thing to check, since you said *user-assigned*: `DefaultAzureCredential` with no arguments will pick the system-assigned identity, or fail ambiguously if several are attached. Tell it which one:

```python
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

cred = DefaultAzureCredential(managed_identity_client_id="<user-assigned-client-id>")
client = BlobServiceClient("https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net", credential=cred)
```

If you get `AuthorizationPermissionMismatch` after fixing both, decode the token your app actually got (`cred.get_token("https://storage.azure.com/.default")`) and check the `oid` claim against the principal you assigned the role to. Propagation is usually under five minutes; an hour of waiting means it is not propagation.

203/EXEC means the child process was forked and `execve()` failed. The script's own permissions are fine — something about the exec itself differs. In order of likelihood:

**1. The interpreter is not on systemd's PATH.** `#!/usr/bin/env node` resolves `node` through `PATH`, and a service gets a fixed minimal `PATH`: `/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin`. It does not read `~/.bashrc`, `~/.profile` or `/etc/profile`, so an nvm- or asdf-installed Node under `/home/worker/.nvm/versions/...` is invisible. Your shell has it because your login session sourced the profile.

**2. CRLF line endings.** A script saved on Windows has a shebang of `#!/usr/bin/env node\r`, and the kernel looks for an interpreter literally named `node\r`. `file /opt/worker/run.sh` says `with CRLF line terminators`; `sed -i 's/\r$//' run.sh` fixes it.

**3. A non-executable or non-traversable parent directory**, or `/opt` mounted `noexec`. `namei -l /opt/worker/run.sh` shows every component; `findmnt -T /opt/worker` shows the mount options.

Fixes, in order of preference:

```bash
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/node /opt/worker/run.js
User=worker
```

An absolute interpreter path in the unit removes the shebang from the equation entirely. If you must keep the shebang:

```bash
[Service]
Environment=PATH=/home/worker/.nvm/versions/node/v22.11.0/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
ExecStart=/opt/worker/run.sh
```

To see the real errno rather than guessing:

```bash
journalctl -u worker -b --no-pager -o verbose
systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/worker.service
systemd-run --uid=worker --pty /opt/worker/run.sh
```

`systemd-run` reproduces the failure in systemd's environment interactively and prints the actual message. It is the fastest way to tell case 1 from case 2. Note also that sandboxing options (`ProtectHome=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `PrivateTmp=`) can make a path unreachable to the service and only to the service — if you have any of those set, comment them out to bisect.

`/etc/security/limits.conf` is read by `pam_limits.so`, which runs as part of a **PAM session**. A login shell, an `ssh` session and `su` all set one up; a service started by systemd does not go through PAM at all, so that file is simply never consulted. Your shell's 65535 is real and completely irrelevant to the unit.

For a service the limits come from the unit (or systemd's defaults):

```bash
[Service]
LimitNOFILE=65535
```

Then:

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart worker      # restart, not reload — limits are set at fork time
cat /proc/$(pgrep -f worker.js)/limits | grep 'open files'
```

`LimitNOFILE=65535` sets soft and hard to the same value. `LimitNOFILE=1024:65535` sets soft:hard separately, which matters if the process raises its own soft limit at runtime.

Two details that catch people:

**Node uses the soft limit.** libuv never bumps it for you, so a hard limit of 1M with a soft limit of 1024 still gives you EMFILE at 1024. Whatever you set, check the first column of `/proc/PID/limits`, not the second.

**If you did not edit the unit, where did 1024/4096 come from?** From `DefaultLimitNOFILE` in `/etc/systemd/system.conf` or a drop-in — some distro or config-management packages set it low. Grep for it:

```bash
systemctl show worker -p LimitNOFILE -p LimitNOFILESoft
grep -r DefaultLimitNOFILE /etc/systemd/
```

`systemctl show` is authoritative: it tells you what systemd will actually apply, after all drop-ins.

Finally, if you genuinely need tens of thousands of descriptors, check the system ceiling too — `sysctl fs.file-max` and `fs.nr_open`; `LimitNOFILE` cannot exceed `fs.nr_open` (1048576 by default, so usually fine). And 65535 open files for a worker writing chunk files is worth a second look — an unclosed stream in an error path produces exactly this symptom, and raising the limit only moves the crash later.

Two separate things are going on, and the empty log file is the more interesting one.

**Why the log is empty.** The redirect is performed by the shell cron spawns, before your script runs. If `/var/log/backup.log` does not exist and `deploy` cannot create files in `/var/log` (root-owned, mode 755), the shell fails at `>>` and the command never executes. There is no output because nothing ran, and the shell's error message went to cron's mail — which the `No MTA installed, discarding output` line tells you was thrown away.

Point the log somewhere the user owns:

```bash
30 2 * * * /home/deploy/backup.sh >> /home/deploy/backup.log 2>&1
```

or `sudo touch /var/log/backup.log && sudo chown deploy: /var/log/backup.log`.

**Why it would fail even then.** Cron gives the job a minimal environment: `PATH` is `/usr/bin:/bin` (set in `/etc/crontab` or compiled in), `HOME` and `SHELL` are set, and nothing else. Your login shell's `PATH` came from `/etc/profile` and `~/.profile`, which cron does not read. So `/usr/local/bin/aws` and `/usr/local/bin/pg_dump` are not found. `~/.aws/config`, `~/.pgpass` and `PGPASSWORD` are the same class of problem — anything exported from a profile is absent.

Fix at the top of the crontab:

```bash
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
30 2 * * * /home/deploy/backup.sh >> /home/deploy/backup.log 2>&1
```

To see what the job actually gets, run this once and read the output:

```bash
* * * * * env > /home/deploy/cron-env.txt 2>&1
```

Diff that against your interactive `env` and every difference is a candidate cause.

One more crontab-specific trap: `%` is not a literal in a crontab line — it is translated to a newline and everything after the first one becomes stdin for the command. If your script call ever contains `date +%F`, escape it as `\%F`.

Rather than reverse-engineering cron's environment for every job, make the script not depend on it. Three lines at the top and it behaves identically under cron, systemd, and your shell:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail
exec >> /home/deploy/backup.log 2>&1
export PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
export HOME=/home/deploy
echo "=== $(date -Is) starting ==="
```

`exec >>` moves the redirect *inside* the script, so it runs as your user with your permissions, and — importantly — the log now captures the failure of the script itself rather than the shell failing to open the file. `set -Eeuo pipefail` makes it stop at the first failing command instead of running `aws s3 cp` on a dump that was never written. Then the crontab line is just:

```bash
30 2 * * * /home/deploy/backup.sh
```

If you want the failure to be visible rather than sitting in a file nobody reads, drop cron and use a systemd timer. You get logs in the journal, exit status in `systemctl status`, and no environment guessing:

```bash
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.service
[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=deploy
Environment=PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
ExecStart=/home/deploy/backup.sh

# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers backup.timer
journalctl -u backup.service -n 50
```

`Persistent=true` runs a missed schedule after a reboot, which cron will not do. `systemd-run --uid=deploy --pty /home/deploy/backup.sh` reproduces the run interactively in the same environment when you need to debug it.

Your suspicion is right. `unlink()` removes the directory entry; the inode and its blocks are freed only when the last open file descriptor to it closes. `du` walks directory entries, so it cannot see the file. `df` asks the filesystem how many blocks are allocated, so it does. That gap is exactly the deleted-but-open file.

Confirm and find the holder:

```bash
$ sudo lsof +L1
COMMAND   PID   USER  FD  TYPE DEVICE     SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME
node     2891 deploy  11w  REG  259,1  92341207040     0  655 /var/log/app.log (deleted)
```

`+L1` lists open files with a link count below 1, i.e. exactly the deleted ones. `NLINK` of 0 and the `(deleted)` suffix confirm it. `SIZE/OFF` is your missing 87 GB.

Reclaim it without restarting by truncating through `/proc`:

```bash
sudo truncate -s 0 /proc/2891/fd/11
```

`/proc/PID/fd/N` is a symlink to the inode itself, so truncating it releases the blocks immediately — `df` updates on the spot. The process keeps writing to the same descriptor and does not notice.

The caveat: the file offset is not reset. The process is at byte 92341207040 and will keep writing there, so the file will immediately report that size again. It is now sparse, so it costs almost nothing on disk, but `ls -l` will look alarming and any tool that reads it from the start will churn through 87 GB of zeros. That is usually acceptable as an emergency measure; plan a restart at a convenient time to actually reset the offset.

The permanent fix is to stop deleting live log files. Either configure logrotate with `copytruncate` (same truncation, done properly), or — better — have logrotate rename the file and signal the process to reopen it:

```bash
/var/log/app.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    compress
    missingok
    notifempty
    postrotate
        systemctl reload app.service
    endscript
}
```

Best of all, log to stdout and let journald or your container runtime own rotation; then there is no file for anyone to `rm`.

Before you go hunting for open descriptors, run the three checks that separate the four common causes of `df` and `du` disagreeing — the deleted-file one is the most famous but not the only one, and the others need entirely different fixes.

**1. Reserved blocks.** ext4 reserves 5% of the filesystem for root by default. Non-root writes fail with ENOSPC while `df` still shows a few GB used by that reserve, and `Avail` reads 0 while `Used` is less than `Size`.

```bash
sudo tune2fs -l /dev/nvme0n1p1 | grep -i 'reserved block count'
sudo tune2fs -m 1 /dev/nvme0n1p1     # 1% instead of 5%, applies immediately
```

On a 100 GB data volume this is 5 GB you can have back. Do not do this on the root filesystem of a machine you care about — the reserve exists so root can still log in and fix things.

**2. Inode exhaustion.** ENOSPC is also returned when there are no free inodes, and then `df -h` looks healthy.

```bash
df -i /
```

`IUse%` at 100% means millions of tiny files somewhere — usually a session or cache directory.

**3. A mountpoint shadowing data.** If something was written to `/var/lib/data` *before* the volume was mounted there, those files still occupy the root filesystem and are invisible while the mount is active. `du` cannot see them either.

```bash
sudo mkdir /mnt/root && sudo mount --bind / /mnt/root
sudo du -xh --max-depth=2 /mnt/root | sort -h | tail -20
sudo umount /mnt/root
```

The bind mount exposes the underlying root tree with nothing mounted over it. This one is invisible to `lsof` and to every "disk full" guide that only covers deleted files.

**4. Deleted-but-open files** — `sudo lsof +L1`, and if that is what it is, truncate `/proc/PID/fd/N`.

Note `du -sh /` without `-x` also crosses into `/proc`, `/sys` and other mounts, which makes the number meaningless; use `sudo du -xh --max-depth=1 /` for a comparison you can trust against `df`.

The resource ARN is wrong. `arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads` identifies the *bucket*. `s3:PutObject` acts on an *object*, whose ARN is `arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads/<key>`. A bucket ARN never matches an object-level action, so the statement allows nothing at all for PutObject.

That is also exactly why `s3:ListBucket` works with the same ARN — `ListBucket` is a bucket-level action, so the bucket ARN is the correct resource for it. The two action families take different resource shapes and this catches everyone once.

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "BucketLevel",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetBucketLocation"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ObjectLevel",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:DeleteObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads/*"
    }
  ]
}
```

Note `arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads/*` does not include the bucket itself, so you need both statements — a single `Resource` list with both ARNs works too, but splitting them keeps the action/resource pairing obvious.

You can verify without redeploying, using the simulator against the actual role:

```bash
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/app-ec2 \
  --action-names s3:PutObject \
  --resource-arns 'arn:aws:s3:::my-app-uploads/test.txt' \
  --query 'EvaluationResults[].EvalDecision'
```

You mention a second suspicion, and you are right to have it: with SSE-KMS and a customer managed key, the fixed policy above still fails, because PutObject additionally requires KMS permissions on the key. Fix the ARN first, retry, and if you still get AccessDenied it is the key — see the KMS side separately.

Assuming you have already noticed the missing `/*` on the resource ARN, the second cause is the one your last sentence hints at, and it produces an identical, unhelpful `AccessDenied` from `PutObject`.

With default encryption set to SSE-KMS using a **customer managed key**, S3 does not encrypt with the key directly. It calls `kms:GenerateDataKey` on your behalf, using *your* credentials. If the role cannot call that action on that key, the upload fails, and the error surfaces as S3 AccessDenied with no mention of KMS.

Two policies have to allow it — the IAM policy on the role:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["kms:GenerateDataKey", "kms:Encrypt", "kms:DescribeKey"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:eu-central-1:123456789012:key/1a2b3c4d-...",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": "s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com" }
  }
}
```

and the **key policy** on the CMK itself, which is a resource policy and is evaluated independently — an IAM allow does not grant access to a KMS key whose policy does not mention your principal (unless the key policy delegates to IAM with the standard `"Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root"}` statement, which is what the default key policy does; a hand-written one often does not).

Add `kms:Decrypt` as well if the same role ever reads objects back — S3 needs it to unwrap the data key on GetObject, and multipart uploads need it too.

How to tell the two causes apart definitively: look at CloudTrail. An IAM/ARN problem shows an `AccessDenied` on `eventSource: s3.amazonaws.com`, `eventName: PutObject`. A KMS problem shows a *successful-looking* S3 call preceded by an `AccessDenied` on `eventSource: kms.amazonaws.com`, `eventName: GenerateDataKey`, with the key ARN in `resources`.

```bash
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=GenerateDataKey \
  --max-results 5 --query 'Events[].CloudTrailEvent' --output text | head
```

The `kms:ViaService` condition above is worth keeping: it means a leaked role credential can use the key through S3 but not to decrypt arbitrary ciphertext directly.

An internet gateway routes traffic for instances that have a **public IP**. It performs 1:1 NAT between a public IP and a private one; a packet from an address with no public IP mapping has no source address to translate to, so it is dropped. Lambda ENIs never get a public IP — you cannot assign one, and there is no setting for it. So an IGW route in a subnet full of ENIs without public IPs is a black hole, which is exactly the timeout you are seeing.

Outbound internet from a Lambda in a VPC requires a NAT gateway (or a NAT instance) in a **public** subnet, with the private subnets' route table pointing default traffic at it:

```bash
# public subnet's route table
0.0.0.0/0  ->  igw-0abc...

# the two private subnets' route table (the one the Lambda uses)
0.0.0.0/0  ->  nat-0def...
10.0.0.0/16 -> local
```

Verify before redeploying — find the ENIs the service created for your function, then follow their subnets to the route table actually in effect:

```bash
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --filters Name=description,Values="AWS Lambda VPC ENI*" \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[].{eni:NetworkInterfaceId,subnet:SubnetId,sg:Groups[0].GroupId}'

aws ec2 describe-route-tables \
  --filters Name=association.subnet-id,Values=subnet-0123,subnet-0456 \
  --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[]'
```

The trap in that second command: if it returns nothing, the subnets have no explicit association and are using the VPC's **main** route table — which is very likely not the one you edited. Check `--filters Name=association.main,Values=true` in that case.

Two more things to confirm at the same time: the NAT gateway must sit in a subnet whose route table points at the IGW (a NAT gateway in a private subnet is a common and silent mistake), and it needs an Elastic IP. Egress security group rules were never the issue — you already have allow-all, and the RDS connection proves the ENIs are wired up.

Also lower the HTTP client timeout below the function timeout. Right now the 30s you see is Lambda giving up, which tells you nothing; a 5s connect timeout in the client would have surfaced a clean `ETIMEDOUT` in your own logs with a stack you control.

Adding a NAT gateway fixes it, and it is the standard answer, but it is worth knowing what you are signing up for and what the alternatives are — NAT gateway is roughly $32/month per AZ plus a per-GB data processing charge on *all* traffic through it, and for HA you want one per AZ.

**If the destination were an AWS service**, you would not need NAT at all: a VPC endpoint keeps the traffic on the AWS network. Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free; interface endpoints (Secrets Manager, KMS, SQS, and most others) are hourly-priced but usually cheaper than NAT and strictly more secure, since the traffic never touches the internet.

```bash
aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id vpc-0abc \
  --service-name com.amazonaws.eu-central-1.s3 \
  --route-table-ids rtb-0123
```

For a third-party HTTPS API there is no endpoint, so that is out — unless the vendor offers PrivateLink, which some do; worth one email.

**The other direction is to question the VPC placement itself.** You put the function in a VPC to reach RDS. If the only thing you need from RDS is queries, consider whether the reverse split is cheaper: keep the outbound-calling function outside the VPC, and have it talk to a second, VPC-attached function (or an SQS queue consumed by one) that owns database access. Two functions, no NAT gateway, and the database stays private. The cost is an extra hop and an extra cold start on the DB path.

If the third-party calls are rare and the RDS work is constant, that split is clearly worth it. If it is the other way round, put in the NAT gateway and stop thinking about it.

One thing not to do: making the RDS instance publicly accessible so the Lambda can leave the VPC. It works, it is cheap, and it puts your database on the internet behind nothing but a security group.

Assuming you have already added `logs:CreateLogGroup`/`CreateLogStream`/`PutLogEvents` and the group still is not there, there are three other reasons a running function has no log group, all of which look identical from `describe-log-groups`.

**1. You are looking in the wrong region.** Log groups are regional, and the CLI uses whatever region your profile defaults to, which is often not the function's. Ask the function:

```bash
aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name my-fn \
  --query '{region: FunctionArn, logging: LoggingConfig}'
```

**2. The function has a custom log group configured.** Lambda's advanced logging controls let you send output somewhere other than `/aws/lambda/<name>`. If `LoggingConfig.LogGroup` in the output above is set to something else, that is where your logs are — and the prefix search you ran would never find it. Same block also carries `LogFormat` (`Text` or `JSON`) and `ApplicationLogLevel`; if the level is set to `WARN` and your code only calls `console.log`, the stream exists but is empty.

**3. An SCP or a permissions boundary denies it.** An explicit `Deny` in a Service Control Policy at the account or OU level overrides any `Allow` in the role, and a permissions boundary on the role caps its effective permissions to the intersection. Both are invisible in the role's attached policies. Check with the simulator, which evaluates the whole chain:

```bash
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-fn-role \
  --action-names logs:CreateLogGroup logs:PutLogEvents \
  --resource-arns 'arn:aws:logs:eu-central-1:123456789012:log-group:/aws/lambda/my-fn:*'
```

`implicitDeny` means nothing granted it; `explicitDeny` means an SCP or boundary is blocking it and no amount of editing the role's policy will help.

While you are in there: `LogFormat: JSON` is worth turning on. It gives you structured fields (`requestId`, `level`, `timestamp`) that CloudWatch Logs Insights can query without a parse expression, and it costs nothing.

Yes — Container Apps ingress defaults `targetPort` to 80, and the platform's probe connects to that port. Your container listens on 8080, nothing accepts on 80, every probe fails, and the revision never leaves `Activating` with 0 healthy replicas.

Fix it in place, no redeploy of the image needed:

```bash
az containerapp ingress update -n api -g rg-prod --target-port 8080
```

Or, if you manage the app as YAML:

```bash
properties:
  configuration:
    ingress:
      external: true
      targetPort: 8080
      transport: auto
```

`targetPort` is the port *inside* the container. Ingress always terminates on 443/80 externally regardless — you do not need to change anything on the public side.

A more robust option, if you would rather the port not be duplicated in two places: read it from the environment. Container Apps injects a `PORT` variable and your app can bind to it, which also makes the same image work unchanged on Cloud Run and App Service.

```javascript
const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 8080;
app.listen(port, '0.0.0.0', () => console.log(`Listening on 0.0.0.0:${port}`));
```

Then set `targetPort` once and it matches whatever the platform asks for.

Two things to confirm while you are there. Bind to `0.0.0.0`, not `localhost` — your log line already shows you do, but a container listening only on 127.0.0.1 produces exactly the same stuck-`Activating` symptom, and it is the second most common cause. And if you have defined explicit `probes` in the app spec, they carry their own `port` field which does **not** inherit from `targetPort`; changing ingress alone will not fix those.

On the second half of your question — yes, you can see the probe failure directly instead of inferring it from `Activating`. There are two log streams and the one you want is the system stream, not the console stream.

```bash
az containerapp logs show -n api -g rg-prod --type system --follow
```

`--type system` gives you the platform's own events: image pull, container start, probe results, replica scheduling, and the reason a revision was deactivated. `--type console` (the default) gives you your app's stdout, which in your case looks perfectly healthy and tells you nothing.

The revision object also carries a failure reason that `az containerapp revision list` truncates away:

```bash
az containerapp revision show -n api -g rg-prod --revision api--abc123 \
  --query 'properties.{state:runningState,healthState:healthState,error:provisioningError}'
```

If the environment is wired to Log Analytics (the default for a managed environment), the same data is queryable and retained, which is more useful than `--follow` for something that failed overnight:

```sql
ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
| where ContainerAppName_s == "api"
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| project TimeGenerated, RevisionName_s, Reason_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc
```

`Reason_s` will read something like `ContainerRestarting` or a probe failure, with the port in `Log_s`.

Worth knowing for next time: with no `probes` block, Container Apps applies a default TCP readiness probe against the ingress `targetPort`. That is why a wrong `targetPort` and a genuinely broken app are indistinguishable from the revision state alone — the system log is the only place the difference shows up.

The `httpRequest.latency` on a Cloud Run request log is measured by the front end and includes everything: container start, your module-level work, and the handler. To split it, compare that log entry's timestamp against the timestamps of your container's own stdout, since those are separate log entries with their own clocks on the same trace.

Query the two streams together in Logs Explorer:

```bash
resource.type="cloud_run_revision"
resource.labels.service_name="my-service"
(logName:"run.googleapis.com%2Frequests" OR logName:"run.googleapis.com%2Fstdout")
```

Sort ascending and read the gaps for one cold request:

- **request log `receiveTimestamp`** → **your first stdout line**: this is image pull, sandbox creation, and the Node runtime booting before any of your code has produced output. This is the platform's share.
- **first stdout line** → **your "listening" line**: your module-level work — the Cloud SQL connect and the cache warm.
- **"listening"** → **request completed**: the handler itself, ~40 ms as you know from warm requests.

To make the second boundary crisp, print a timestamp as the very first statement of your entry module and again after warm-up:

```javascript
console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'boot', up: process.uptime() }));
await warmCache();
console.log(JSON.stringify({ msg: 'ready', up: process.uptime() }));
```

`process.uptime()` starts when the Node process starts, so `boot` tells you how much of the 9 s was gone before your code ran at all, and `ready - boot` is precisely your own startup work. No trace correlation needed.

Cloud Trace shows the request span but does not break out container startup as a child span, so it will not give you this boundary — the two-timestamp method above is the reliable one.

In my experience with a 480 MB image the platform share is typically 1–3 s (Cloud Run streams layers lazily, so image size matters less than the layer count and the size of what is actually read at start), and a Cloud SQL connect plus a cache warm is very easily the other 6+. Measure before optimising: people routinely spend a day slimming an image to save 800 ms of a 9 s problem.

Once you have the split, the two levers are different and it is worth knowing which applies.

**Startup CPU boost** is the single highest-value setting for this shape of problem. By default a container gets its configured CPU allocation; with boost it gets more CPU during startup, which cuts Node's module-loading and any JIT-heavy warm-up substantially.

```bash
gcloud run services update my-service --cpu-boost --region europe-west1
```

**Move the warm-up off the startup path.** Connecting to Cloud SQL and warming a cache at module load means every cold start pays for both before the first request can be served. Make them lazy and let the first request pay only for what it needs:

```javascript
let poolPromise;
const getPool = () => (poolPromise ??= createPool());

app.get('/thing/:id', async (req, res) => {
  const pool = await getPool();
  res.json(await lookup(pool, req.params.id));
});
```

If the cache warm exists to avoid a slow first query rather than to be correct, it belongs behind a lazy getter or a background `queueMicrotask` after `listen()`, not in front of it.

**Image size.** Cloud Run streams layers on demand, so 480 MB is not 480 MB of latency — but it is not free either. A multi-stage build against `node:22-slim` or distroless typically lands under 150 MB for a Node service:

```bash
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .

FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app /app
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

**Min instances** does not fix the cold start, it hides it — and it is the correct answer surprisingly often. One idle instance costs roughly the price of a small VM and eliminates the tail latency entirely for a service with steady traffic. Do the other three first, then decide whether the residual is worth paying for.

Yes, this is an encoding mismatch in the canonical request. V4 signing builds a string that includes the canonical resource path, and the signature only verifies if the path in the URL that GCS receives is byte-for-byte what you signed.

The rule for GCS V4: in the canonical request the object name is percent-encoded with `/` left unescaped, and **every other reserved character escaped**, including space as `%20` and `+` as `%2B`. The URL you hand out must use the same encoding. The failure mode you hit is almost always one of:

- The object name went into the URL raw or with `quote_plus`, so a space became `+`. GCS decodes `+` in a path as a literal plus, not a space, so it looks up a different object *and* computes a different canonical path — the signature fails first.
- The path was encoded with the default `safe='/'` in one place and `safe=''` in the other.

Do not build the path yourself. The client library gets this right:

```python
from datetime import timedelta
from google.cloud import storage

client = storage.Client()
blob = client.bucket("my-bucket").blob("reports/q3 summary+final.pdf")

url = blob.generate_signed_url(
    version="v4",
    expiration=timedelta(minutes=15),
    method="GET",
)
```

Pass the object name **decoded** — the real name as it exists in the bucket, spaces and pluses and all. `generate_signed_url` does the canonicalisation and the URL escaping consistently. The common bug is passing an already-encoded name, which produces a double-encoded path (`%2520`) that also fails, so check that too.

If you must construct it, encode once with:

```python
from urllib.parse import quote
canonical = "/" + bucket + "/" + quote(object_name, safe="")
```

`safe=""` (not the default `safe="/"`) — GCS's V4 spec escapes `/` inside the object name as `%2F` in the canonical resource for signed URLs generated this way, so mixing the two conventions between signature and URL is the other half of this bug class.

Quick isolation test: sign the same object under a temporary copy with a plain ASCII name. If that URL works, it is encoding and not credentials.

Before assuming it is encoding, rule out the other two producers of `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, because both are common and neither is fixed by touching the object name.

**1. The signature was produced by the wrong key or by IAM SignBlob.** `SignatureDoesNotMatch` says "the signature does not correspond to the request as signed by that key". If your code runs somewhere with no downloaded key file — GCE, GKE, Cloud Run — `storage.Client()` gets credentials from the metadata server, which has no private key. The library then has to sign through the IAM API, and that needs to be set up explicitly:

```python
import google.auth
from google.auth import compute_engine
from google.auth.transport import requests as grequests

credentials, _ = google.auth.default()
credentials.refresh(grequests.Request())

signing_credentials = compute_engine.IDTokenCredentials(
    grequests.Request(), "", service_account_email=credentials.service_account_email
)
```

and the signing service account needs `roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` **on itself**. Without it you get an error at signing time, but with a partially-configured setup you can get a URL that is generated and simply does not verify. Since you said "service account key", check that the key file you loaded belongs to the account you think — `json.load(open(path))["client_email"]` — and that the key has not been disabled in IAM.

**2. Extra or missing headers.** The signature covers a specific set of headers. If the URL is fetched by something that adds a header you included in `headers=` when signing, or the client sends a different `Host` (a custom domain, a load balancer, `storage.googleapis.com` vs `<bucket>.storage.googleapis.com`), the canonical request differs and the signature fails. Sign for the exact host the client will use.

**3. Clock skew** produces `RequestTimeTooSkewed` rather than a signature mismatch, so 15 minutes of expiry is not your problem here — but note V4 caps expiry at 7 days and silently longer values are rejected.

Isolate in one step: generate a signed URL for an object with a plain name using the same credentials in the same process. Works → the object name encoding is the bug. Fails → the credentials/signing path is, and the object name is a red herring.

The metadata server returning the default compute service account is the diagnosis: the node pool is not running the GKE metadata server. Workload Identity has to be enabled in **two** places, and the annotation is only the third of three required pieces.

1. Workload Identity on the cluster (sets the workload pool):

```bash
gcloud container clusters update my-cluster --region europe-west1 \
  --workload-pool=my-proj.svc.id.goog
```

2. The GKE metadata server on the **node pool**. This is the step that is usually missed, because enabling it on the cluster does not retrofit existing pools:

```bash
gcloud container node-pools update default-pool \
  --cluster=my-cluster --region europe-west1 \
  --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA
```

Until this is set, pods talk to the raw GCE metadata endpoint and get the node's own service account — exactly what you observed. Note this recreates nodes.

3. The IAM binding on the Google service account, granting the Kubernetes service account permission to impersonate it:

```bash
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  data-reader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member="serviceAccount:my-proj.svc.id.goog[my-namespace/my-ksa]"
```

The member string is literal syntax: workload pool, then `[namespace/kubernetes-serviceaccount-name]` in square brackets. A typo here fails silently — the annotation is honoured, the impersonation is refused, and you fall back to an error rather than a wrong identity.

Verify from inside a pod after restarting it:

```bash
kubectl exec -it mypod -- curl -sH 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' \
  'http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/email'
```

It must print `data-reader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. If it still prints the compute default, step 2 has not taken effect on the node your pod landed on.

Adding to the cluster/node-pool/IAM checklist — three things that keep the metadata server returning the wrong identity even when all three are configured correctly.

**The pod is not using the service account you annotated.** The annotation lives on a ServiceAccount object; a pod that does not name one gets `default` in its namespace. Check the pod, not the manifest you think you applied:

```bash
kubectl get pod mypod -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'
kubectl get sa <that-name> -o yaml | grep iam.gke.io
```

If it says `default`, add `serviceAccountName: my-ksa` to the pod template. This is the single most common cause after the node-pool flag.

**The pod has not been restarted.** The identity is resolved when the pod's token is issued; annotating the ServiceAccount does nothing for running pods. `kubectl rollout restart deploy/...`.

**`hostNetwork: true` bypasses the GKE metadata server.** Pods on the host network reach the node's real metadata endpoint, so they always get the node service account regardless of any annotation. There is no workaround other than not using host networking for that pod.

Also worth checking: the namespace in the IAM member string must match the pod's actual namespace, and the binding is on the *Google* service account, not the project. A binding added at project level with `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` does nothing.

Once the identity is right and you still get 403, then it genuinely is the bucket IAM — and note `roles/storage.objectViewer` granted at the **project** level and at the **bucket** level are different policies. Confirm which one you set:

```bash
gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy gs://data-lake \
  --format='table(bindings.role, bindings.members)'
```

Uniform bucket-level access must be enabled for bucket IAM to apply cleanly; with legacy ACLs in play, an object can be unreadable despite a correct role binding.

Your diagnosis is correct and it is the whole story. `lodash` on npm ships CommonJS. `import { debounce } from 'lodash'` is compiled to something equivalent to `require('lodash')` followed by a property access, and `lodash/index.js` requires all 300-odd modules to build its export object. Tree shaking works on the ES module graph: webpack has to see static `export` statements to know which bindings are unused. With `module.exports = ...` there is nothing static to analyse, so every module stays.

Two working options:

**`lodash-es`** — the same library published as ES modules, with `"sideEffects": false` in its package.json:

```bash
npm rm lodash && npm i lodash-es
```

```javascript
import { debounce } from 'lodash-es';
```

Bundle cost drops to roughly 2–3 kB for `debounce` and its internals. Note `lodash-es` is ESM-only, so if the same code runs under Jest or plain Node CommonJS you will need transform configuration there.

**Deep import from `lodash`** — works with the CJS package, no new dependency:

```javascript
import debounce from 'lodash/debounce.js';
```

This requires exactly one module and its transitive requires, so the other 290 never enter the graph. Slightly uglier, zero migration risk. (Avoid the `lodash.debounce` standalone package — it is deprecated and has not been updated in years.)

On `sideEffects: false` in your own package.json: it applies only to **your** modules, telling webpack it may drop your files whose exports are unused. It says nothing about `lodash`, so it does not help here at all. It is still worth setting if your own code is side-effect-free, with the usual caveat that a bare `import './styles.css'` is a side effect and must be excluded:

```json
{
  "sideEffects": ["*.css", "*.scss"]
}
```

`optimization.usedExports: true` is already implied by `mode: 'production'`, so that line is redundant either way.

Two things in the snippet are worth separating, because conflating them is what makes this hard to debug.

**`splitChunks` and dynamic import do different jobs.** A dynamic `import()` always produces its own chunk — that is unconditional, it does not need configuration and cannot be disabled by config. `splitChunks` operates *afterwards*, deciding whether modules shared between chunks get pulled into common ones. So "no second chunk was emitted" is never a `splitChunks` problem. Tuning `minSize`, `chunks`, `cacheGroups` will not help until an async boundary exists.

**A dynamic import whose result is never used is still split.** You verified the arrow function is called, but that was not necessary: webpack splits on the syntactic presence of `import()`, not on reachability.

So work backwards from the module graph rather than from the config. Ask webpack what it saw:

```bash
npx webpack --profile --json > stats.json
node -e "const s=require('./stats.json'); console.log(s.chunks.map(c=>[c.id,c.names,c.initial,Math.round(c.size/1024)+'kb']))"
```

One chunk with `initial: true` and nothing else confirms it. Then check whether `./Editor` is even in the graph as an async dependency:

```bash
node -e "const s=require('./stats.json'); console.log(s.modules.filter(m=>/Editor/.test(m.name)).map(m=>({n:m.name,reasons:m.reasons.map(r=>r.type)})))"
```

A `reason` of `cjs require` or `harmony import specifier` means it was pulled in statically; `import()` would show as `import()` in the reason type. That is a definitive answer in one command, without guessing at which transpiler did it.

Also confirm webpack is reading the config you are editing — the snippet in your question mixes application source (`const Editor = ...`) with `module.exports = {...}` in what looks like one file. If those really are the same file, that file is not your webpack config, and webpack is running on defaults with no `splitChunks` block at all. `npx webpack --config webpack.config.js --stats detailed` prints the resolved config path.

`eval` is development-only, and more specifically: it emits **no `.map` file at all**. It wraps each module in `eval()` with a `//# sourceURL` comment, which is why DevTools can show you separate module files in dev but stack traces in a production build point at the bundle. The `.map` files sitting next to your bundles are stale leftovers from an earlier config — check their mtime.

For production you want a value that produces a real, separate map file:

```javascript
module.exports = {
  mode: 'production',
  devtool: 'source-map',
};
```

The devtool names are a grammar, not a list, which is why there appear to be twenty of them. Read them as `[inline-|hidden-|eval-][nosources-][cheap-[module-]]source-map`:

- `eval` — no file, dev only, fastest rebuild
- `inline` — the map is base64'd into the bundle, so no separate file; do not use in production, it doubles the download
- `hidden` — the map is emitted but no `//# sourceMappingURL` comment is added
- `nosources` — the map has line/column mappings but no original source text
- `cheap` — line-level mappings only, no columns
- `module` — map back through loaders to the original file rather than to the loader's output

For a production TypeScript build there are only two sensible choices: `source-map` (full fidelity, slowest build) and `hidden-source-map` (identical output, no comment). `cheap-module-source-map` is a reasonable dev choice but in production it gives you the right line and the wrong column, which on a minified single-line bundle is close to useless.

Make sure TypeScript is also emitting maps, or webpack has nothing to map back to:

```bash
{ "compilerOptions": { "sourceMap": true } }
```

`ts-loader`/`babel-loader` pass their maps through and webpack composes them, but only if the loader produced one.

Once you have switched off `eval` and are emitting real maps, there is a second failure mode worth knowing, because it produces the identical symptom: the map is emitted, served with 200, and the browser still shows you the bundle.

Things that silently defeat a correct source map:

**DevTools has them turned off.** Settings → Preferences → Sources → "Enable JavaScript source maps". It is on by default but gets toggled off and stays off. Check this first — it costs five seconds and explains a surprising share of these reports.

**The map is served with the wrong content type or behind auth.** A `.map` returned as `text/html` (a SPA fallback route catching the 404) or a 401 from a protected CDN path is ignored without any console message. DevTools does log it under the Console's "Verbose" level, which is filtered out by default:

```bash
curl -sI https://example.com/static/main.4f21.js.map | head -3
```

You want `200` and `application/json`. A 200 with `text/html` means your server is returning `index.html` for the map — that is a routing bug, and it looks exactly like "source maps do not work".

**The `sourceMappingURL` comment was stripped.** Some CDN transforms, some post-build minifier steps and some Docker `COPY` patterns drop the last line of the file. Confirm it survived:

```bash
tail -c 120 dist/main.4f21.js
```

**Paths in the map do not resolve.** Webpack writes `webpack://project/./src/app.ts` by default, which DevTools shows as a virtual path — fine for reading, but "open in editor" and some tools need real relative paths. `output.devtoolModuleFilenameTemplate` controls this:

```javascript
output: {
  devtoolModuleFilenameTemplate: 'webpack://[namespace]/[resource-path]?[loaders]',
}
```

Finally, if the frame reads `main.4f21.js:1:88213` in a **logged** stack — from `error.stack` sent to your backend — no source map will help. `Error.prototype.stack` is generated from the running bundle, and maps are applied by DevTools at display time, not by the engine. Resolving those requires applying the map server-side (`source-map` npm package) or letting your error tracker do it.

On "is there any risk in widening it" — yes, and it is the reason the prefix exists rather than being a Vite quirk.

`import.meta.env.VITE_X` is not a lookup. Vite performs a textual replacement at build time, so this:

```javascript
fetch(`${import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL}/users`)
```

becomes this in `dist/assets/index-8f2a.js`:

```javascript
fetch(`https://api.example.com/users`)
```

The value is a string literal in a file you serve to the public. The prefix is an opt-in marker meaning "I have decided this value is public".

Widening the prefix means every matching variable in the environment becomes a candidate for inlining. Set `envPrefix: ''` and you have opted your entire `.env` in — and `.env` files in real projects contain `DATABASE_URL`, `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY`, `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`. Worse, in CI the process environment often holds the whole secret store, and Vite reads process env in addition to `.env` files. Vite actually refuses an empty `envPrefix` for this reason, but a prefix like `APP_` that happens to match something sensitive is accepted without complaint.

Keep `VITE_`, or add one narrow extra prefix and treat anything carrying it as published.

The related design question, since an API URL is what prompted this: because the value is baked at build time, one build artifact cannot be promoted from staging to production if the URL differs. If you want that — and you generally do — read it at runtime instead:

```javascript
// index.html
<script>window.__CONFIG__ = { apiUrl: "__API_URL__" };</script>
```

and substitute `__API_URL__` at container start, or serve a small `/config.json` the app fetches before boot. Then the same image runs in every environment and no URL is compiled into the JavaScript. `import.meta.env` stays for genuinely build-time things: `MODE`, feature flags, the release SHA.

The option is `base`. It is the public path every generated asset URL is prefixed with, and it defaults to `/`: ```javascript // vite.config.ts export default defineConfig({ base: '/dashboard/', }); ``` Both slashes matter: leading, because it is an absolute path from the domain root, and trailing, because Vite concatenates rather than joins. `base: '/dashboard'` yields `/dashboardassets/index-8f2a.js`. You can also set it per build without editing the config, which is useful if the same code deploys to different prefixes: ```bash vite build --base=/dashboard/ vite preview --base=/dashboard/ ``` To answer the second half directly — yes, `base` covers all three of the places assets get referenced, because Vite rewrites them during the build rather than relying on the browser's resolution: - `

There is a second option with a different trade-off: `base: './'`, which emits relative URLs.

```javascript
export default defineConfig({
  base: './',
});
```

`index.html` then contains `src="./assets/index-8f2a.js"`, and the app works under any prefix without knowing what it is — the domain root, `/dashboard/`, `/preview/pr-482/`, a `file://` path, an Electron app. One build artifact, deployable anywhere. That is genuinely valuable if your preview deployments live under per-PR paths, or if the mount point is a customer configuration.

The catch, and it is a real one: relative URLs resolve against the **current document URL**, not against where `index.html` lives. With client-side routing and history mode, a user who loads `https://example.com/dashboard/settings/profile` directly gets a document at that path, and `./assets/index.js` resolves to `/dashboard/settings/assets/index.js` — 404. The app works from `/dashboard/` and breaks on deep links and on refresh.

So:

- **SPA with history routing** → use an absolute `base` (`'/dashboard/'`). The prefix is known at build time anyway, and deep links must work.
- **Hash routing, or a single page with no client-side routes** → `'./'` is fine and buys you portability, because the path portion of the URL never changes.
- **Unknown prefix plus history routing** → `'./'` plus a `<base href="/dashboard/">` tag injected into `index.html` at serve time. The `<base>` element fixes relative resolution for the document, and you can substitute it at container start. More moving parts, but it is the only combination that gives you both.

If you go absolute, `--base` at build time keeps a single config working for multiple targets:

```bash
vite build --base="/preview/pr-${PR_NUMBER}/"
```

The mixed export is the cause in your case; here is the rest of the list, since these all produce the same `page reload` line and people usually hit two or three of them over a project's life.

**Anonymous default export.** Fast Refresh identifies components by name; an unnamed one has no stable identity across edits.

```typescript
export default () => <Panel />;              // reloads
const Panel = () => <div />;                  // fine
export default Panel;
```

**Component name not in PascalCase.** `export function panel()` is treated as a plain function, not a component, so the module is a mixed-export module by the rule above.

**A hook exported alongside a component.** `export function usePanel()` next to `export function Panel()` is the same problem as a constant — one of the exports is not a component.

**HOC-wrapped exports.** `export default memo(Panel)` and `export default connect(...)(Panel)` are frequently not recognised, depending on plugin version. `memo` and `forwardRef` are handled by current `@vitejs/plugin-react`; arbitrary third-party HOCs are not. Export the inner component too, or apply the HOC at the call site.

**Exporting types is fine** — `export type Props = {...}` is erased before the plugin sees it, as long as it is a type-only export. `export { type Props, Panel }` also works; `export const enum` does not.

One thing that is easy to misread: **the file named in the reload message is not always the file you edited.** Vite propagates an HMR update up the import graph until it finds a module that accepts it. If your edit is in `Panel.tsx` but the message names a parent, the parent is where the chain broke. Here it names `Panel.tsx` itself, so the problem is in that file — but when the two differ, fix the file in the message.

If the constant genuinely belongs in that file and you do not want a second module for one string, you have two options with different costs.

**Keep it and accept the reload.** For a file you edit rarely this is fine. The cost is only paid when *that* file changes.

**Take manual control of the HMR boundary.** Vite's API lets a module declare that it can accept its own updates, which stops the invalidation propagating:

```typescript
export function Panel() { /* ... */ }
export const PANEL_ID = 'panel';

if (import.meta.hot) {
  import.meta.hot.accept();
}
```

This is a blunt instrument and I would not reach for it in application code — you are telling Vite "re-execute this module and everything is fine", which is true for a constant and false the moment someone adds state or a side effect to the file. React state in the component will still be lost because Fast Refresh is not doing the update; the module is simply re-evaluated. It buys you a faster refresh, not preserved state.

Worth being precise about what you are actually losing, because it changes how much this matters. A full reload costs you: React state, scroll position, focus, and anything in memory. It does not cost you anything persisted. If the state you keep losing is form input, the durable fix is to persist it (URL params, `sessionStorage`) rather than to depend on HMR — that also helps the user who reloads the page.

For the common case, though, moving the constant is one line and permanent:

```bash
mkdir -p src/components/panel
git mv src/components/Panel.tsx src/components/panel/Panel.tsx
echo "export const PANEL_ID = 'panel';" > src/components/panel/constants.ts
```

A file per component with its non-component exports beside it is a shape that keeps Fast Refresh working without anyone having to remember the rule.

Jest's default `transformIgnorePatterns` is `["/node_modules/", "\\.pnp\\.[^\\\\/]+$"]`, so nothing under `node_modules` reaches ts-jest and `nanoid`'s ESM arrives at Node's CJS loader verbatim. Carve it out with a negative lookahead:

```json
{
  "preset": "ts-jest",
  "testEnvironment": "node",
  "transformIgnorePatterns": [
    "node_modules/(?!(nanoid)/)"
  ]
}
```

Read it as: ignore paths containing `node_modules/` **unless** what follows is `nanoid/`. For several packages, alternate them:

```json
"transformIgnorePatterns": ["node_modules/(?!(nanoid|@sindresorhus|escape-string-regexp)/)"]
```

Two things that make this fail in practice:

**The pattern is matched against the absolute path.** With pnpm, modules live at `node_modules/.pnpm/nanoid@5.0.7/node_modules/nanoid/`, and `node_modules/(?!nanoid/)` matches the *first* `node_modules/` — which is followed by `.pnpm/`, not `nanoid/`, so the file is ignored. For pnpm you need `node_modules/(?!\\.pnpm/)` or a pattern accounting for the store layout.

**ts-jest must be willing to transform a `.js` file.** By default the preset only maps `.ts`/`.tsx`. Add JS to the transform, or the carve-out lets the file through to a transformer that does not handle it:

```json
{
  "transform": {
    "^.+\\.[tj]sx?$": ["ts-jest", { "tsconfig": { "allowJs": true } }]
  }
}
```

On why the default is an ignore pattern rather than an allow-list: transforming `node_modules` is expensive — a real project has tens of thousands of files there, and Jest would have to parse and cache all of them. Skipping the directory wholesale was the right default when nearly everything shipped CJS. It ages badly now that packages are going ESM-only, which is why the lookahead trick is so widespread.

The laziest fix, and often the right one for `nanoid` specifically: mock it.

```javascript
// jest.setup.js
let counter = 0;
jest.mock('nanoid', () => ({ nanoid: () => `test-id-${++counter}` }));
```

```json
{
  "preset": "ts-jest",
  "testEnvironment": "node",
  "setupFilesAfterEnv": ["<rootDir>/jest.setup.js"]
}
```

The module is never loaded, so it is never parsed, so the syntax error cannot happen — and you get deterministic ids, which is almost certainly what you want in tests anyway. Snapshot tests with real nanoid values fail on every run; that is a problem you have not hit yet but will.

This obviously only applies to dependencies whose behaviour you do not need to exercise. `nanoid` qualifies: you are not testing that it generates unique strings, that is its job and it has its own tests.

If you do need the real thing and want zero configuration, the other escape hatch is pinning:

```bash
npm i nanoid@3
```

nanoid 3.x is the last CJS release. It is still maintained for security fixes and its API is identical for the `nanoid()` call. That is a legitimate choice for a project that is not going to migrate to ESM soon — you are trading being one major behind for not carrying a transform config. Check the changelog before doing this on a package where the majors differ meaningfully; for nanoid they do not.

Both of these are worse than fixing the transform if the project is long-lived and more ESM-only dependencies are coming. Both are better if this is the only one and you want it off your desk today. Mark the choice so the next person knows it was deliberate:

```javascript
// nanoid pinned to 3.x (last CJS release) to avoid an ESM transform config.
// Revisit when the suite moves to ESM or Vitest.
```

Check where the test file lives. `jest.mock('./api')` resolves the path **relative to the file that calls it** — the test file — not relative to the module under test.

If your layout is:

```bash
src/api.js
src/profile.js
src/__tests__/profile.test.js
```

then `profile.js` requires `./api` → `src/api.js`, while the test's `jest.mock('./api')` refers to `src/__tests__/api.js`. Jest registers a mock for a module that does not exist (with a factory, it does not need to exist — that is why you get no error), `src/api.js` is never mocked, and the real one loads. Meanwhile your test's `import { fetchUser } from './api'` would fail to resolve... unless your `moduleDirectories`/`roots` config makes it resolve elsewhere, which is exactly the kind of thing that turns this into a twenty-minute puzzle.

Fix by pointing at the same module the code under test uses:

```javascript
jest.mock('../api', () => ({ fetchUser: jest.fn(() => ({ id: 1 })) }));
```

Or co-locate the test as `src/profile.test.js`, where `./api` means the same thing from both files. Co-location removes this whole class of bug permanently.

Confirm which module the registry actually mocked:

```javascript
console.log(require.resolve('./api'));   // from the test file
```

Run that at the top of the test and compare it against the path `profile.js` resolves. If they differ, that is your answer.

To be explicit about your last question: no, the CommonJS `require` in `profile.js` is not the problem. `jest.mock` replaces the entry in Jest's module registry, and `require('./api')` reads from that registry — so a correctly-targeted mock is picked up by a module-scope `require` exactly as it is by an `import`. Hoisting is also working as you expect: babel-jest moves the `jest.mock` call above the transpiled `require` calls in the test file.

The cleaner structural answer is that waiting for infrastructure is not the test suite's job. Jest starts when the environment is ready; making it ready belongs to the CI job.

GitHub Actions service containers have health checks built in, and the job does not start your steps until they pass:

```bash
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      minio:
        image: minio/minio:latest
        ports: ['9000:9000']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "curl -f http://localhost:9000/minio/health/live"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 3s
          --health-retries 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
```

Docker retries the health command up to 20 times at 5 s intervals; the runner blocks until the container reports healthy or gives up. By the time `npm test` runs, the service is accepting connections, and the 5000 ms default is fine again.

If the thing you start is not a service container — a compose stack, a binary — the same principle applies as one step before the tests:

```bash
- run: docker compose up -d
- run: timeout 90 bash -c 'until curl -sf http://localhost:9000/health; do sleep 1; done'
- run: npm test
```

Two advantages over polling inside Jest. The failure is attributed correctly: a red "wait for service" step reads as an infrastructure problem, whereas a red test reads as a code problem and sends the next person reading the diff in the wrong direction. And the wait happens once for the whole run rather than once per worker — Jest runs test files in parallel processes, and a `beforeAll` in each of six files means six independent polls.

Keep a short assertion inside the suite anyway (`expect(await health()).toBe(200)` as the first test) so a mid-run failure is still diagnosable. But the waiting itself belongs in the job.

One edge case that makes raising the timeout actively counterproductive: if the failure is a hung connection rather than slow work, a longer Jest timeout only means you wait longer for a message that tells you nothing.

`Exceeded timeout of 5000 ms for a test` is Jest reporting that a promise never settled. It cannot tell you *why*, because it does not know what the promise was doing. Meanwhile the real error — `ECONNREFUSED`, a TLS handshake failure, a 503 — is sitting inside a client that was never given a timeout of its own and will happily wait forever.

Give every network call in tests a deadline shorter than the Jest timeout, so the client's error surfaces first:

```javascript
const res = await fetch(url, {
  body: stream,
  method: 'POST',
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8_000),
});
```

With `AbortSignal.timeout` (Node 18+) the failure becomes `TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout` with a stack pointing at the call site, or better, the real `ECONNREFUSED` if the container is simply not there. Both are actionable; "exceeded timeout" is not.

The same applies to database and SDK clients — `connectTimeout`/`requestTimeout` for `pg`, `requestHandler` timeouts for the AWS SDK, `connectTimeoutMS` for Mongo. Set them in the test config, not just production.

Two other CI-specific things worth doing while you are here:

```bash
npm test -- --runInBand
```

A GitHub-hosted runner has 2 (sometimes 4) vCPUs. Jest defaults to `cpus - 1` workers, and if each worker opens its own connections to one container you get contention that does not exist on your 10-core laptop — which is a very common source of "only flaky in CI". `--runInBand` (or `--maxWorkers=2`) often makes a suite both faster and stable on small runners.

And set `CI=true` (Actions does this already) — Jest disables the watch prompt and some interactive behaviour, and several libraries reduce retry noise.

Before settling on a fix, one correction that changes how much this matters: **"Jest did not exit" is a warning, not a failure.** Jest prints the results, sets exit code 0, and then waits. Your CI job is green — and then sits there holding a runner until the job-level timeout (6 hours by default on GitHub Actions) or until the runner is reclaimed.

So the cost is not a red build, it is burned CI minutes and a job that looks stuck. That is worth fixing properly rather than papering over, and it is also why nobody noticed it for a while.

Second correction: the frame `--detectOpenHandles` prints is where the handle was *created*, which is often not where the import chain started. `src/server.ts:22` listening means something imported `src/server.ts`. Find out what:

```bash
grep -rn "from ['\"].*server['\"]" src/ test/
grep -rn "require(['\"].*server['\"])" src/ test/
```

Frequently it is a transitive import — a test imports a route module, which imports a middleware, which imports `server` for a config export. In that case the fix is to move the shared value out rather than to touch the test.

Also worth knowing about `--detectOpenHandles`:

- It forces `--runInBand`, so the run is much slower and timing-dependent handles may not reproduce.
- It only catches handles created through async_hooks-instrumented APIs. Native addons and some libraries create handles it cannot see, so an empty report does not prove there is no leak.

When it reports nothing but Jest still hangs, bisect instead:

```bash
npx jest --runInBand --listTests | while read f; do
  timeout 60 npx jest --runInBand "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "HANGS: $f"
done
```

Crude, but it finds the file in one pass, and then you read that file's imports.

Related but different: `--detectLeaks` is about memory retention between test files, not open handles. It is experimental and produces false positives; do not reach for it here.

If you decide to use `--forceExit` anyway — and there are situations where it is the correct call, such as a legacy suite you are not going to refactor this quarter — make it a deliberate, visible decision rather than a flag someone adds to `npm test` and forgets.

Put it in the config with a comment naming what it is covering and when it comes out:

```javascript
// jest.config.js
module.exports = {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  // Temporary: src/server.ts listens on import, leaving a TCPSERVERWRAP handle.
  // Remove once the app/entry-point split lands (see #482).
  forceExit: true,
};
```

And pair it with the check that keeps it honest, so the underlying leak cannot grow while it is hidden:

```bash
- run: npm test
- run: npx jest --detectOpenHandles --runInBand 2>&1 | tee handles.log
- run: |
    count=$(grep -c '^  ●  ' handles.log || true)
```
